scenes.tts: Why does a small nudge fade, while a slightly bigger one fires a full spike?
scenes.visual: The near-threshold traces from chapter 1: two small bumps that fade and one that becomes a spike. The question appears above.
scenes.narration: Why does a small nudge fade, while a slightly bigger one fires a full spike?

scenes.tts: Nudge the membrane 5 millivolts, to minus 60. A few sodium channels open, and a little sodium flows in.
scenes.caption: Nudge the membrane 5 mV, to −60 mV. A few sodium channels open, and a little sodium flows in.
scenes.visual: A tally panel labelled illustrative units. A 5 mV nudge from −65 to −60 mV. An orange inward arrow labelled 2.
scenes.narration: Nudge the membrane 5 mV, to −60 mV. A few sodium channels open, and a little sodium flows in.

scenes.tts: Potassium current flows out. Leak is still inward here, below its equilibrium potential. Together they give more outward current.
scenes.visual: A purple outward arrow for potassium and a small grey inward arrow for leak combine into one outward arrow labelled 3 (potassium plus leak).
scenes.narration: Potassium current flows out. Leak is still inward here, below its equilibrium potential. Together they give more outward current.

scenes.tts: Net current is outward, so the voltage drifts back. Nothing happens.
scenes.visual: Net arrow: 1 outward. The trace decays back to rest.
scenes.narration: Net current is outward, so the voltage drifts back. Nothing happens.

scenes.tts: Now nudge it 12 millivolts, to minus 53. More sodium channels open, and inward current beats outward.
scenes.caption: Now nudge it 12 mV, to −53 mV. More sodium channels open, and inward current beats outward.
scenes.visual: Second tally at −53 mV, same illustrative units: inward 6, outward 4 (potassium plus leak). Net inward.
scenes.narration: Now nudge it 12 mV, to −53 mV. More sodium channels open, and inward current beats outward.

scenes.tts: The voltage rises, which opens still more sodium channels. Inward current grows faster than potassium and leak can oppose it.
scenes.visual: The inward arrow grows faster than the outward arrow as the voltage climbs; a feedback loop spins. The trace runs away into a spike.
scenes.narration: The voltage rises, which opens still more sodium channels. Inward current grows faster than potassium and leak can oppose it.

scenes.tts: That is threshold. Past it, sodium feedback sustains itself, and the rise runs away.
scenes.visual: Label: threshold = the point past which sodium feedback sustains itself.
scenes.narration: That is threshold. Past it, sodium feedback sustains itself, and the rise runs away.

scenes.tts: Inward current at one instant is not enough. What matters is whether sodium keeps outgrowing the opposing currents.
scenes.visual: Small note on screen: net inward current alone is not the definition.
scenes.narration: Inward current at one instant is not enough. What matters is whether sodium keeps outgrowing the opposing currents.

scenes.tts: So threshold is not a fixed voltage. A slow depolarization inactivates sodium channels and opens potassium channels, raising it.
scenes.visual: A slow ramp creeps up; inactivation gates close along the way, and the dashed threshold line rises ahead of it.
scenes.narration: So threshold is not a fixed voltage. A slow depolarization inactivates sodium channels and opens potassium channels, raising it.

scenes.tts: Once the rise sustains itself, the spike runs its course. Its size is set by the channels and the equilibrium potentials.
scenes.visual: A spike draws to completion with the scale beside it. Labels: channels, E_Na, E_K.
scenes.narration: Once the rise sustains itself, the spike runs its course. Its size is set by the channels and the equilibrium potentials.

scenes.tts: With brief pushes from rest, a bigger push brings the spike sooner. Its size stays essentially the same. That is all-or-none.
scenes.visual: Overlaid spikes from brief small and large stimuli: roughly equal heights (not identical), the larger stimuli earlier. Label: all-or-none.
scenes.narration: With brief pushes from rest, a bigger push brings the spike sooner. Its size stays essentially the same. That is all-or-none.

scenes.tts: Right after a spike, most inactivation gates are shut. No stimulus, however strong, fires a second spike. That is the absolute refractory period.
scenes.visual: Paired-pulse sequence. Right after the first spike, a row of sodium channel cartoons shows their slow gates shut. A strong second pulse gives only a small graded bump, no second spike. Label: absolute refractory, no second spike.
scenes.narration: Right after a spike, most inactivation gates are shut. No stimulus, however strong, fires a second spike. That is the absolute refractory period.

scenes.tts: As those gates reopen, a stronger stimulus can fire a spike, often a smaller one. That is the relative refractory period.
scenes.visual: Slow gates reopen one by one. A stronger second pulse now fires a smaller spike. Label: relative refractory.
scenes.narration: As those gates reopen, a stronger stimulus can fire a spike, often a smaller one. That is the relative refractory period.

scenes.tts: A stronger push is needed then, because some sodium channels are still inactivated and potassium conductance is still raised.
scenes.visual: Two labels beside the smaller spike: some Na+ channels still inactivated; g_K still raised.
scenes.narration: A stronger push is needed then, because some sodium channels are still inactivated and potassium conductance is still raised.

scenes.tts: At long intervals, the second spike is full size again.
scenes.visual: A plot builds: second-spike height against interval, zero at short intervals, rising through the relative period, flat at full size.
scenes.narration: At long intervals, the second spike is full size again.

scenes.tts: One more question. Block the potassium channels with T E A. What happens to the falling phase?
scenes.caption: One more question. Block the potassium channels with TEA. What happens to the falling phase?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. Block K+ channels with TEA: what happens to the falling phase?
scenes.narration: One more question. Block the potassium channels with TEA. What happens to the falling phase?

scenes.visual: the question stays on screen

scenes.tts: From the same starting voltage, the rise is little changed. The fall is slower, relying on inactivation and leak, so the spike broadens.
scenes.visual: A broadened spike draws over a dashed normal spike from the same starting voltage. The upstrokes are similar, not an exact overlay; the downstroke is slower.
scenes.narration: From the same starting voltage, the rise is little changed. The fall is slower, relying on inactivation and leak, so the spike broadens.

scenes.tts: The undershoot is shallower too, because it comes from raised potassium conductance.
scenes.visual: The undershoot of the blocked spike is shallower than the dashed normal one.
scenes.narration: The undershoot is shallower too, because it comes from raised potassium conductance.

scenes.tts: Threshold is sodium feedback that sustains itself. Inactivation makes refractoriness. Blocking potassium broadens the spike.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card on screen: Threshold = self-sustaining sodium feedback. Inactivation makes refractoriness. Blocking K+ broadens the spike.
scenes.narration: Threshold is sodium feedback that sustains itself. Inactivation makes refractoriness. Blocking potassium broadens the spike.
